hook: You walk into the kitchen and forget why. You go back to the couch, and it comes back. A word sits on the tip of your tongue until a friend says the first letter. Memories are often stored but stuck. Retrieval is about finding the right cue.

options: Getting stored information back out of memory
prereq.why: Encoding gets it in, storage keeps it, retrieval gets it back out.

prereq.q: Which study plan leads to better long-term memory?
prereq.why: The spacing effect: distributed practice beats massed practice for long-term memory.

figure.caption: Recall needs more from memory than recognition; matching cues help both.

chain.cause: A memory is stored with features of the setting, body state and mood
The same cues are present at the test
chain.effect: retrieval is easier (context-dependent, state-dependent and mood-congruent memory)

chain.cause: Students practice pulling information out of memory
chain.effect: retrieval routes get stronger (the testing effect)
students overestimate what they know, a failure of metacognition

ideas: Recall produces information with few cues; recognition picks it from options, which act as retrieval cues, so it is usually easier.
Retrieval is easier when cues match learning: the place (context-dependent), the body's state (state-dependent), and the mood (mood-congruent).
Retrieval practice (self-quizzing) beats rereading for long-term memory: the testing effect.
Metacognition is judging your own learning. Familiarity from rereading feels like knowing but is not; testing yourself is the honest check.

misconception.wrong: Rereading notes and highlighting until they feel familiar is the best way to study.
misconception.right: Familiarity is not memory. Testing yourself, with the notes closed, builds far stronger long-term memory and shows you what you do not know yet.

summary: Retrieval depends on cues. Recognition is usually easier than recall because the options are cues. Matching the place, body state or mood of learning helps retrieval. Practicing retrieval (the testing effect) strengthens memory more than rereading, and good metacognition means checking what you know by testing yourself instead of trusting familiarity.
